claims.claim: As of 2026-10-06, the commercial de minimis exemption is suspended for low-value shipments across modes; formal or informal entry and applicable duties/fees are required, and the August 13, 2026 CIT decision upheld the de minimis rescission notwithstanding the Supreme Court's separate invalidation of IEEPA tariffs.
claims.counterevidence: The Supreme Court held that IEEPA did not authorize the challenged tariffs, but the CIT expressly stated the de minimis rescission was not decided in that case; the CIT judgment itself may remain subject to appellate review.

claims.claim: Public Law 119-21 repeals the commercial-shipment de minimis exception effective July 1, 2027.
claims.counterevidence: A future Congress could amend the statute before the effective date, but no such change was found in this bounded research.

claims.claim: The importer of record is the central customs-liability role: an eligible party must make entry using reasonable care, and the IOR is required to deposit estimated duties and fees.
claims.counterevidence: Commercial agreements can shift the economic incidence of duties to another party, but that does not by itself change statutory entry responsibility.

claims.claim: A platform that conducts classification, valuation, duty work, or prepares CBP entry documents on behalf of others can enter the customs-business licensing boundary; mere electronic transmission of received data is expressly excluded.
claims.counterevidence: A pre-purchase comparison estimate that is not prepared for or transmitted as a CBP filing is not clearly within the cited definition; exact implementation matters.

claims.claim: For CPSC-regulated imported finished products, certification responsibility is tied to the responsible importer/eligible entry party; CPSC states that an individual consumer purchasing for personal use is not typically treated as the importer responsible for certification, and mandatory eFiling took effect July 8, 2026.
claims.counterevidence: Not every consumer product is subject to a CPSC certification requirement; applicable rules must be determined product by product.

claims.claim: Under the CPSA, a third-party logistics provider that solely receives, holds, or transports goods without taking title, as well as carriers and freight forwarders, is not deemed a manufacturer, distributor, or retailer solely because of those logistics activities.
claims.counterevidence: The statutory protection does not cover additional conduct such as taking title, selling, importing in another capacity, or other activities beyond ordinary logistics.

claims.claim: FCC exposure can arise before a platform becomes importer of record because marketing includes advertising or offering RF devices for sale; for imported devices subject to Supplier's Declaration of Conformity the importer can be the responsible party, while limited personal-use import exceptions exist.
claims.counterevidence: The personal-use exception permits specified categories of three or fewer devices, and whether a passive comparison link itself constitutes prohibited marketing would depend on facts not resolved by the cited rules.

claims.claim: Moving from routing into an online marketplace can trigger INFORM Consumers Act seller-verification, disclosure, suspension and reporting-mechanism duties; federal enforcement against Temu demonstrates this is an enforced boundary.
claims.counterevidence: A comparison service or buying-agent arrangement does not automatically satisfy the statutory definition of an online marketplace; coverage depends on platform and seller relationships.

claims.claim: If a platform itself holds out or operates as an ocean transportation intermediary/NVOCC, separate FMC licensing, financial-responsibility and tariff-related requirements can arise.
claims.counterevidence: Using an already regulated NVOCC or forwarder does not by itself make the technology platform an NVOCC.

claims.claim: A legally plausible light-asset architecture exists in which the platform does not take title or become IOR and outsources customs and transport functions to eligible/licensed parties; regulation does not itself require IOR status merely to aggregate commercial demand.
claims.counterevidence: The research did not establish that carriers or buying agents will grant material volume discounts under this allocation of roles; specific carrier contracts could require a regulated shipper or intermediary.

claims.claim: Architectures E and F represent the clearest regulatory cliff because becoming IOR or inventory-owning importer directly adds customs duty/entry responsibility and, for relevant products, CPSC importer/eFiling and FCC responsible-party obligations.
claims.counterevidence: The exact compliance burden varies by product; certification-based FCC devices can place primary technical responsibility on the certification grantee rather than automatically on every importer.

claims.claim: Community evidence indicates that 2026 CPSC eFiling/certificate requirements are already creating practical documentation friction for buying-agent users, but this does not establish the agent's legal IOR or seller status.
claims.counterevidence: The Reddit account and user comments are not a substitute for authenticated contracts, entry records, or agency determinations.
